mainEntity.name: How much does a Volkswagen e-Golf battery replacement cost?

acceptedAnswer.text: A Volkswagen e-Golf battery replacement typically costs £5,000-£12,000 depending on battery size (24.2kWh or 35.8kWh) and whether you choose a new or reconditioned unit. Individual module replacement: £1,100-£1,500 per module. Reconditioned battery pack: £4,000-£8,000. New battery pack (dealer): £8,000-£12,000. Fitting costs: £500-£1,000 depending on workshop.

mainEntity.name: What is the most common failure on the Volkswagen e-Golf?

acceptedAnswer.text: The most frequently reported issues are: onboard charger (OBC) failure - prevents AC charging; fault code B200000. Battery degradation - range reduction; warranty covers below 70% capacity. HV coolant heater failure - no cabin heat in winter. Electric motor bearing wear - humming/whining noise on high-mileage examples. BMS software issues - 2015-2016 models affected by recall.

mainEntity.name: Is it worth replacing the battery in a Volkswagen e-Golf?

acceptedAnswer.text: It depends on the vehicle's value and condition. A typical e-Golf (2017-2020) is worth £8,000-£16,000. If the car is worth under £8,000 and needs a full battery pack replacement, carefully evaluate against scrappage or part-exchange value. If the car is worth £10,000+, a reconditioned battery pack (£5,000-£8,000) is usually financially viable. If only one or two battery modules have failed, individual module replacement (£1,100-£1,500) is often the most cost-effective solution. If the vehicle is still within the 8-year/100,000-mile warranty and capacity is below 70%, replacement may be free.

mainEntity.name: How long does a Volkswagen e-Golf battery replacement take?

acceptedAnswer.text: A typical Volkswagen e-Golf battery replacement takes 1-3 days for an EV specialist workshop. Battery health diagnostic: 1-2 hours. Individual module replacement: 4-8 hours. Full battery pack replacement: 6-12 hours. Supply & fit lead time: 3-7 working days from quote acceptance to completion.

mainEntity.name: What's the difference between the 24.2kWh and 35.8kWh e-Golf batteries?

acceptedAnswer.text: These are two different battery generations fitted to the e-Golf. 24.2kWh (2014-2016): 264 cells, 323 volts, approx. 118-mile range. 35.8kWh (2017-2020): upgraded chemistry, 159-186-mile range, 100kW motor. Both use passively cooled Panasonic NMC cells. Enter your registration above to confirm which is fitted to your e-Golf.

mainEntity.name: Does a replacement Volkswagen e-Golf component come with a warranty?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes - every reconditioned Volkswagen e-Golf component supplied through EnginesMarket carries a minimum 12-month warranty. Warranty covers manufacturing defects and component failure. All components are tested and verified by EV specialists. historyTimeline.h2: Volkswagen e-Golf - Battery & Motor History at a Glance
historyTimeline.intro: The Volkswagen e-Golf, introduced in 2014, was Volkswagen's first mass-produced all-electric vehicle and a pioneer in the compact EV segment. Based on the Golf Mk7 platform, the e-Golf combined the practicality of the world's favourite hatchback with a zero-emission powertrain. The e-Golf was produced in two distinct battery generations, with a significant mid-life upgrade in 2017 that nearly doubled its usable range. Production ended in 2020, making way for the Volkswagen ID.3 on the dedicated MEB platform.

milestones.description: e-Golf launched with 24.2kWh lithium-ion battery pack, 115hp (85kW) electric motor, approx. 118-mile (190km) range
2016 - Early e-Golf models feature 24.2kWh battery, 85PS/115kW motor, 264 cells, 323 volts
2016 - Recall issued for battery management system software; oversensitive diagnostics could falsely detect electrical surge and shut down electric motor
Major battery upgrade to 35.8kWh lithium-ion pack, range increased to 159 miles (255km WLTP), motor output 136PS (100kW) with 290Nm torque
2020 - Second-generation e-Golf with 35.8kWh battery, 100kW motor, 0-62mph in 9.6 seconds
Onboard charger module issues reported; fault code B200000 related to OBC module
End of e-Golf production; replaced by Volkswagen ID.3

historyTimeline.closingNote: Every major component fitted to the Volkswagen e-Golf is covered below, with UK battery replacement pricing, motor reconditioning costs and known EV-specific failure points.

commonProblems.h2: Volkswagen e-Golf - Battery, Motor & EV System Problems - Repair Cost vs Replacement
commonProblems.h3: The Volkswagen e-Golf is generally a reliable EV, but several well-documented issues can lead to significant repair bills - and in some cases, component replacement is the only viable option. Battery degradation, motor bearing wear, onboard charger failure and HV heater problems are the most common failure points. Every reconditioned component supplied through EnginesMarket comes with a minimum 12-month warranty, and all work is carried out by EV-certified specialists.

problems.h4: Battery Degradation - The e-Golf's Primary Long-Term Concern
problems.affectedModels: Volkswagen e-Golf (all years, especially higher-mileage examples)
problems.rootCause: All lithium-ion batteries degrade over time. The e-Golf's passively cooled battery pack is more susceptible to temperature-related degradation than liquid-cooled systems. Volkswagen's 8-year/100,000-mile warranty guarantees 70% capacity retention, with repairs covered if capacity drops below this threshold.

repairOptions.longevity: If multiple modules have failed or capacity is severely degraded

For vehicles worth under £8,000, a full battery pack replacement may approach or exceed the vehicle's value - carefully evaluate against scrappage or part-exchange value. Individual module replacement (£1,100-£1,500) is usually the most cost-effective solution if only one or two modules have failed.
problems.recommendation: If you notice a significant reduction in range, have a battery health test performed by an EV specialist. If the battery is still under the 8-year/100,000-mile warranty and capacity has dropped below 70%, contact a Volkswagen dealer immediately for a warranty claim. For out-of-warranty vehicles, individual module replacement is often more cost-effective than a full pack replacement.

problems.h4: Onboard Charger (OBC) Failure - The Most Common EV-Specific Fault
problems.rootCause: The onboard charger module can fail, preventing AC charging. Fault code B200000 is the primary indicator. Causes include inadequate cooling, software glitches, or internal component failure.

repairOptions.longevity: First-line fix; may resolve if software-related

problems.recommendation: If your e-Golf won't charge on AC, check the charging cable and charging station first. If those are working, have the OBC diagnosed by an EV specialist. A firmware update may resolve the issue if it's software-related. If the OBC has failed completely, a reconditioned unit from a specialist is significantly cheaper than dealer pricing.

problems.rootCause: The electric motor's bearings can wear over time, producing a humming or whining noise. Voltage sensor faults can also trigger motor shutdown. The motor itself is generally robust, but the EME (motor inverter) can also fail.
